name: Constitutional monarchy
summary: Constitutional monarchism is the defence of constitutional monarchy: a hereditary monarch who is head of state but bound by a constitution and law, with government carried on by responsible ministers and elected assemblies. Its classic theorists present the crown as a neutral power standing above party and opinion (Constant), as the unifying apex of a rational constitutional state (Hegel), or as the 'dignified' part of the constitution that keeps the rights to be consulted, to encourage and to warn (Bagehot); modern advocates defend it as a non-partisan focus of national unity, continuity and the rule of law, and as a safeguard of responsible government.
scope: Constitutional monarchism as the advocacy of constitutional monarchy (s13): the classic theory set out by Benjamin Constant's account of royal power as a neutral power in a constitutional monarchy (s9, tied by s11), Hegel's account of the crown in constitutional monarchy in the Philosophy of Right (s8, tied by s10) and Bagehot's The English Constitution (s3, tied by s12), together with the accounts of constitutional monarchy given by the Monarchist League of Canada and Australians for Constitutional Monarchy (s5, s6, s7) and the scholarship of Hazell and Morris on modern monarchies (s12). Where these sources differ (the crown's veto and Hegel's rejection of popular sovereignty against the parliamentary accounts of Bagehot and the modern leagues), the answer is a split. It excludes absolute and sacral monarchy, legitimist restorationism and the national platforms of the monarchist leagues (their campaigns on symbols, stamps or referendum procedure), which are not tenets of constitutional monarchism.

sources.title: The English Constitution
sources.author: Walter Bagehot
sources.usedFor: The constitutional monarch's three rights, the Queen's lack of a legislative veto, the use of a hereditary monarch, the House of Lords as a revising chamber, the fusion of executive and legislature.

sources.title: A Crown for the 21st Century: Arguments in Support of Canada's Constitutional Monarchy (The Case for the Crown)
sources.author: Monarchist League of Canada
sources.usedFor: The league's account of constitutional monarchy: the sovereign as a non-partisan force of unity, the reserve powers as a safeguard, healthy partisan debate, opposition to an elected president, incremental change, distinct national institutions.

sources.title: How the Monarchy Works
sources.author: Monarchist League of Canada
sources.usedFor: Constitutional monarchy defined: the monarch as referee bound by the constitution and the rule of law, responsible government, reserve powers to cause an election, change by election rather than revolution.

sources.title: Our Identity, Charter and Cause (About ACM)
sources.author: Australians for Constitutional Monarchy
sources.usedFor: Constitutional monarchy as government under a constitution with democratically elected parliaments and independent courts; opposition to a republic; preserving the system as it has evolved.

sources.title: Philosophy of Right, Third Part, The State: Internal Constitution (§§ 260-320)
sources.author: G. W. F. Hegel (1820; Marxists Internet Archive)
sources.usedFor: The crown as apex of constitutional monarchy, hereditary succession, elective monarchy the worst of institutions, rejection of popular sovereignty set against the monarch, the upper house.

sources.title: Du pouvoir royal dans les monarchies constitutionnelles (Principes de politique, 1815, ch. II), in Œuvres politiques, ed. Louandre (1874)
sources.author: Benjamin Constant (Wikisource)
sources.usedFor: Royal power as a neutral power above party and opinion, its rights to dissolve the elective chamber, to veto and to create peers, the inviolable hereditary monarch, hereditary and elective chambers, independent courts.

sources.title: Hegel: Social and Political Thought
sources.author: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.usedFor: Hegel's conception of the crown in terms of constitutional monarchy, the monarch bound by laws and cabinet, gradual reform, rejection of violent popular action, rejection of checks and balances.

sources.usedFor: Modern constitutional monarchs above politics, limited to Bagehot's three rights, a neutral focus of national loyalty, monarchy subject to democracy.

sources.title: constitutional monarchist
sources.author: Wiktionary
sources.usedFor: Defines a constitutional monarchist as a supporter of a constitutional monarchy (the alias).

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Constitutional monarchism keeps a hereditary crown: Hegel grounds the monarch's legitimacy in birth and inheritance, and Constant defends an inviolable hereditary monarch and a hereditary chamber of peers.

democracy-best.rationale: The defining sources split: Australians for Constitutional Monarchy commit to democratically elected parliaments and the Monarchist League of Canada leaves governing to those elected 'as is appropriate in a democracy', while Hegel dismisses sovereignty of the people set against the monarch as a confused notion.

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: The Monarchist League of Canada calls partisan debate 'inevitable and healthy in a vigorous democracy', and Constant presents the neutral crown as letting the disagreements without which no liberty exists develop safely.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The Monarchist League of Canada rejects electing the head of state because it would create another politician and another set of elections, and Hegel rejects any elective monarchy as resting on the caprice of the many.

elective-rulers.rationale: Hegel calls elective monarchy 'the worst of institutions', and the Monarchist League of Canada argues that electing a president or governor general would only create another politician beholden to factions.

gradual-change.rationale: The Monarchist League of Canada credits constitutional monarchy with change that has been 'incremental, and not achieved by violence', and Hegel wants reform to be cautious and gradual, keeping continuity with existing conditions.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: Constant lists the right to dissolve the representative assemblies among the crown's prerogatives as the neutral power, and the Monarchist League of Canada describes parliament as dissolved in the King's name, with reserve powers to force an election.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The defining tenet: Constant, Hegel and Bagehot argue for a hereditary monarch bound by a constitution, and the Monarchist League of Canada and Australians for Constitutional Monarchy defend the crown as head of state while elected ministers govern.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Constant calls the king a neutral power 'superior to the diversity of opinions', and the Monarchist League of Canada presents the sovereign as a non-partisan force of unity who embodies all Canadians, separate from party politics.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Monarchist League of Canada treats partisan debate between parties as healthy in a democracy and places loyalty in the crown rather than in a politician or an ideology, and Australians for Constitutional Monarchy commit to democratically elected parliaments.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The defining sources split: Bagehot says the Queen has no veto and must sign whatever the two Houses send her, while Constant gives the king a veto over the elective chamber and Hegel gives the crown the ultimate decision within the legislature.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The Monarchist League of Canada argues every nation needs to foster its distinct images and institutions, with constitutional monarchy rooted in its history and heritage.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The Monarchist League of Canada defines constitutional monarchy as a monarch who preserves the rule of law within the rules of the constitution, Constant requires that judgments come only from independent courts, and Hegel's monarch acts through universal laws.

second-chamber.rationale: Constant's constitutional monarchy makes laws through a hereditary and an elective chamber, Hegel's legislature has an upper and a lower house, and Bagehot holds that a good revising chamber would be of great benefit.

separated-powers.rationale: The defining sources split: Constant wants separate executive, legislative and judicial powers with a neutral royal power to restore harmony among them, while Bagehot praises the fusion of executive and legislature and Hegel rejects separation of powers for checks and balances.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Australians for Constitutional Monarchy hold that the system as it has evolved should not be tinkered with in the name of theory, and Hegel warns against abolishing customary institutions too quickly.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Mixed: the Monarchist League of Canada says the monarch's first duty is to maintain the laws parliament passes and that he cannot simply impose his will, while Constant makes the hereditary monarch inviolable and not answerable, with ministers responsible instead.

state-harmful.rationale: Hegel holds the state to be absolutely rational and the actuality of the ethical Idea, with the crown at its apex, and the monarchist leagues defend the crown as the central pillar of the state's institutions.

missingStatements.text: The head of state should reign but not rule, acting on the advice of the elected government.
missingStatements.rationale: Bogdanor's formula, quoted in the Wikipedia article, is that a constitutional monarch reigns but does not rule, bound by convention to act on ministerial advice.

missingStatements.text: A head of state who is not elected should keep reserve powers to act in a constitutional crisis.
missingStatements.rationale: Commonwealth realms vest reserve powers in the monarch and governors-general for extreme emergencies, and supporters after the 1975 Australian crisis saw them as a check on elected politicians.
missingStatements.declined: Narrow constitutional detail; monarchy-legitimate and nonpartisan-head-of-state cover the position.

notes: Later pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-12) under rules 5. The first pass rested on two Wikipedia articles and on what adherents of different parties might think; 260 such answers are nulled with their history kept, and the answers now rest on the defining texts: Constant's chapter on royal power in constitutional monarchies, Hegel's Philosophy of Right, Bagehot's The English Constitution, the Monarchist League of Canada's and Australians for Constitutional Monarchy's accounts of constitutional monarchy, the IEP on Hegel, the Encyclopedia of Libertarianism on Constant and Hazell and Morris. Themes searched: government (head of state, succession, election, parliament, veto, dissolution, second chamber, rule of law, separation of powers, democracy), means (revolution, gradual reform), society and culture (heritage, religion, national unity), world (Commonwealth), economy, liberty, ecology and technology. Constitutional monarchism is a doctrine of the head of state and the constitution: its sources take no position on economics, social policy, foreign policy, ecology or technology, so those themes stay null and the uncertainty rule is expected to fail. Blocked to scripted access (named for the maintainer): UCL's Constitution Unit briefing 'What is constitutional monarchy and what is its role in the UK?' and Hazell's chapter in UCL Discovery (Cloudflare block), the Southampton thesis eprints.soton.ac.uk/426243 (bot check), and Bogdanor's Gresham College lecture 'Queen Elizabeth II' (403). Strands differ: Hegel and Constant keep the crown a veto or the ultimate decision, Bagehot and the modern leagues a monarch who reigns but does not rule; where they disagree the answer is 0 at low.
